questions.stem: Choose the meaning of LUCID as used in the sentence: 'Even in the grip of high fever, the old professor gave a LUCID explanation of the theorem to his students.'

options.option_text: expressed in a clear and understandable way
delivered with an elevated and poetic literary style
spoken with great urgency despite physical weakness
composed of intricate technical terminology only

questions.explanation: A is correct. 'Lucid' (Latin 'lucidus' = full of light, bright, clear) means perfectly intelligible and easy to follow. The sentence credits the explanation's quality — clarity — despite the professor's fever. Option C ('great urgency despite physical weakness') is the trap: the fever detail is vivid, but the sentence attributes no urgency to the professor; it praises the explanation's comprehensibility. Rule: In contextual questions, identify what property the sentence is attributing to the word's referent — here, 'explanation' needs a quality, and only clarity fits. Memory hook: LUCID dream = a dream in which you remain fully aware and clear-headed. Example: 'The barrister gave a lucid summary that even the non-specialist jurors could follow.'

questions.stem: Choose the meaning of FRIVOLOUS as used in the sentence: 'The judge dismissed the petition, calling it a FRIVOLOUS attempt to waste the court's valuable time.'

options.option_text: having no serious purpose or genuine legal merit
filed urgently due to time-sensitive legal deadlines
presented without adequate supporting documentary proof
motivated by personal animosity between the rival parties

questions.explanation: A is correct. 'Frivolous' (Latin 'frivolus' = of little weight or value) in legal English denotes a claim that lacks any genuine factual or legal basis. The judge's phrase 'waste of court's time' directly signals absence of merit. Option D ('personal animosity') is tempting because grudge-driven suits are common, but animosity speaks to motive, whereas 'frivolous' speaks to the claim's merit — or total lack of it. Rule: 'Frivolous' in law = baseless, regardless of the filer's sincerity. Example: 'The consumer forum rejected the frivolous complaint as no defect was found in the product at all.'

questions.stem: Choose the meaning of VOLATILE as used in the sentence: 'The political situation in the border district remained VOLATILE, with fresh protests erupting every few days.'

options.option_text: tense and prone to sudden and unpredictable change
thoroughly monitored by central government agencies
improving gradually after months of careful mediation
shaped by deep ideological divisions between rival factions

questions.explanation: A is correct. 'Volatile' (Latin 'volatilis' = flying, fleeting) in figurative use means liable to rapid and unpredictable change. The clue 'protests erupting every few days' signals sudden, unforeseeable flare-ups — the defining feature of volatility. Option D ('deep ideological divisions') is the near-miss: polarisation can fuel protests, but it implies stable, entrenched positions, not sudden eruptions. 'Volatile' captures the unpredictable, explosive quality that 'divided' does not. Rule: The contextual clue verb matters — 'erupting' points to sudden, uncontrolled bursts, which is precisely what volatility means. Memory hook: Volatile chemicals evaporate unexpectedly — a volatile situation 'vapourises into unrest' without warning.

questions.stem: Choose the meaning of DEFUNCT as used in the sentence: 'The committee recommended shutting the DEFUNCT public-sector unit that had not produced a single item in over a decade.'

options.option_text: no longer existing or in any active operational use
running at well below its original production capacity
recently privatised and transferred to new management
undergoing court-ordered financial restructuring and audit

questions.explanation: A is correct. 'Defunct' (Latin 'defunctus' = having finished one's duty, dead) means completely non-operational — not merely struggling. The contextual proof is absolute: 'not produced a single item in over a decade.' Zero output = defunct. Option B ('running well below its original capacity') is the classic distractor because a struggling PSU is a familiar scenario in India, but 'defunct' rules out any production at all, while B implies the unit is still partially running. Rule: 'Defunct' signals complete cessation, not reduced function. Example: 'The defunct National Textile Corporation mill was converted into a housing complex after decades of closure.'

questions.stem: Choose the meaning of PRECIPITATE as used in the sentence: 'Economists warned that any hasty hike in fuel prices could PRECIPITATE a sharp economic slowdown.'

options.option_text: cause something harmful to happen abruptly and prematurely
prevent an economic crisis through well-timed policy action
slow the pace of industrial output across all major sectors
speed up the recovery of markets and restore investor trust

questions.explanation: A is correct. 'Precipitate' as a verb (Latin 'praecipitare' = to hurl headlong) means to bring about an unwanted outcome suddenly and before it would naturally occur. 'Hasty hike' signals recklessness; 'sharp slowdown' signals the negative consequence. Option D ('speed up recovery') is the sophisticated trap: both 'precipitate' and 'accelerate' involve speed, but 'precipitate' exclusively collocates with harmful, premature outcomes — crisis, conflict, collapse — never desirable acceleration. Rule: As a verb, 'precipitate' always implies recklessness and a negative result. Example: 'The unexpected resignation of the finance minister precipitated a steep fall in the stock market within hours.'

questions.stem: Choose the meaning of TENDENTIOUS as used in the sentence: 'The documentary was widely criticised for its TENDENTIOUS portrayal of the conflict, which consistently favoured one side.'

options.option_text: biased so as to promote a single particular viewpoint
factually inaccurate owing to poor journalistic research
emotionally compelling but weak on documentary evidence
visually striking yet shallow in its narrative development

questions.explanation: A is correct. 'Tendentious' (from Latin 'tendentia' = inclination, leaning) describes writing or media that is slanted to advance a particular cause, often controversially. The phrase 'consistently favouring one side' is the precise contextual proof. Option C ('emotionally compelling but evidence-light') is the hard trap: tendentious content is often both emotional and under-evidenced, but a film can be sentimental without being one-sided. The sentence isolates one-sidedness — bias — as the problem, not sentimentality. Rule: 'Tendentious' implies deliberate promotional slant — stronger than 'opinionated' and distinct from merely inaccurate. Example: 'The election manifesto was condemned as tendentious because it ignored all data contradicting the ruling party's record.'

questions.stem: Choose the meaning of INVETERATE as used in the sentence: 'As an INVETERATE traveller, she had explored more than sixty countries before she turned forty.'

options.option_text: deeply habituated over many years to a particular pursuit
enthusiastic about travel but having begun only in recent years
professionally certified and licensed as a tourism consultant
financially independent and capable of affording frequent trips

questions.explanation: A is correct. 'Inveterate' (Latin 'inveteratus' = of long standing, hardened by age) describes a habit so deeply rooted through prolonged practice that it is unlikely to change. The contextual proof is 'sixty countries before forty' — a pattern accumulated over a lifetime, not a recent phase. Option B ('having begun only in recent years') directly contradicts the etymology: 'inveterate' requires duration, so 'recent' is antithetical to its meaning. Option D (financial independence) explains ability, not the deeply-ingrained habitual quality the word carries. Rule: 'Inveterate' always implies long-standing, deep-rooted habituation — it is never applied to new or developing interests. Memory hook: INVETERATE ≈ VETERAN — both share the idea of long experience hardened over time. Example: 'He was an inveterate reader who had not missed a single day without a book in three decades.'

questions.stem: The rupee was VOLATILE throughout the trading session, swinging between gains and losses within hours. What does VOLATILE mean as used in this sentence?

options.option_text: moving within a narrow and predictable range
fluctuating sharply and unpredictably in value
declining steadily over the entire trading day
recovering quickly after an initial sharp fall

questions.explanation: B is correct. The sentence's own clue — 'swinging between gains and losses within hours' — defines VOLATILE as erratic, unpredictable movement. VOLATILE comes from Latin 'volatilis' (flying, fleeting), implying rapid, directionless change. Option C (declining steadily) is tempting but implies a clear downward direction, whereas VOLATILE implies no fixed direction at all. Grammar rule: context clues within the same sentence override any single dictionary sense; 'swinging between' signals erratic oscillation, not trend. Another example: 'His VOLATILE mood shifted from laughter to anger in seconds.'

questions.stem: The new collector took a PRAGMATIC approach to flood relief — bypassing lengthy paperwork and directly distributing supplies. What does PRAGMATIC mean as used here?

options.option_text: guided by practical results rather than rigid procedure
driven by compassion and deep personal concern for victims
bold and willing to take considerable personal risk
strictly following official rules and due administrative process

questions.explanation: A is correct. The sentence shows the collector choosing outcome (distributing supplies) over process (paperwork) — that is the hallmark of PRAGMATIC thinking. From Greek 'pragma' (deed, action), PRAGMATIC means focused on what works. Option B (compassion) wrongly attributes the motive to emotion rather than efficiency; the sentence gives no emotional signal. Option D is the opposite — the sentence explicitly says he bypassed procedure. Grammar rule: when a sentence contrasts the action taken against 'official process' or 'theory,' the contextual meaning of PRAGMATIC is outcome-driven practicality. Another example: 'A PRAGMATIC surgeon selects the fastest safe technique, not the textbook one.'

questions.stem: The OSTENSIBLE motive for the company's donation was public welfare, but investigators later found the funds were used to launder money. Choose the meaning of OSTENSIBLE as used here.

options.option_text: the genuine motive confirmed by independent inquiry
the stated or apparent motive, possibly hiding the truth
a surprising motive revealed only after deep investigation
the selfish motive that was obvious to all outside observers

questions.explanation: B is correct. OSTENSIBLE describes the surface-level, presented reason that may not reflect reality — confirmed here by the contrast 'but investigators found.' From Latin 'ostendere' (to show, display); what is ostensibly shown is the public face, not necessarily truth. Option A (genuine motive confirmed) is the direct opposite. Option C confuses the hidden true motive with the stated one; OSTENSIBLE always refers to what is shown outwardly. Grammar rule: whenever a sentence uses a contrast marker like 'but' or 'however' after a stated reason, the word before it that qualifies that reason is OSTENSIBLE (appearing true, possibly not). Another example: 'His ostensible reason for leaving early was a headache, but his colleagues suspected it was anger.'

questions.stem: Despite court orders and government appeals, the RECALCITRANT landowners refused to vacate the designated wildlife corridor. Choose the meaning of RECALCITRANT as used here.

options.option_text: stubbornly defiant and wilfully resistant to authority
emotionally distressed and deeply confused by the order
financially unable to comply with the relocation terms
deeply committed to environmental and wildlife conservation causes

questions.explanation: A is correct. RECALCITRANT describes deliberate, wilful defiance of legitimate authority. The sentence emphasises 'despite court orders AND government appeals' — both layers of authority were ignored, signalling choice, not inability. From Latin 'recalcitrare' (to kick back), like a stubborn mule resisting the harness. Option C (financially unable) is the most tempting distractor because inability could explain non-compliance, but RECALCITRANT always implies wilful refusal, never incapacity. Option D is an ironic red herring — the landowners' resistance is against vacating, not for conservation. Grammar rule: RECALCITRANT carries the sense of agency and defiance; inability requires a different word (unable, incapacitated). Another example: 'The RECALCITRANT defendant refused to answer even basic questions under oath.'

questions.stem: The documentary became MAUDLIN in its final act, with slow-motion footage and swelling music reducing every scene to an exercise in forced tears. What does MAUDLIN mean here?

options.option_text: technically polished and cinematically sophisticated
darkly pessimistic and philosophically nihilistic in tone
excessively sentimental to the point of feeling tearfully artificial
deliberately provocative in its underlying political messaging

questions.explanation: C is correct. The phrase 'exercise in forced tears' is the contextual anchor — it signals emotion that is manufactured and excessive rather than authentic. MAUDLIN means weakly, tearfully sentimental beyond what the subject warrants. Word origin: from 'Magdalene' (Mary Magdalene), depicted weeping in medieval paintings; 'maudlin drunk' originally meant a weepy, self-pitying drunk. Option A (polished) is opposite in tone. Option B (nihilistic) confuses dark pessimism with sentimental excess — MAUDLIN is weepy, not bleak. Grammar rule: when a sentence uses 'forced,' 'artificial,' or 'exercise in' alongside emotional imagery, the contextual meaning is MAUDLIN (sentimental without restraint). Another example: 'His MAUDLIN farewell speech drew more eye-rolls than sympathy from the audience.'

questions.stem: The report was labelled TENDENTIOUS by the opposition because it cited only data supporting the government's infrastructure policy, ignoring contradictory evidence. Choose the meaning of TENDENTIOUS.

options.option_text: excessively detailed and therefore difficult to read quickly
slanted to promote one viewpoint through selective use of facts
internally inconsistent and riddled with clear logical gaps
overly optimistic while ignoring all legitimate counterarguments

questions.explanation: B is correct. TENDENTIOUS describes writing that deliberately cherry-picks evidence to advance a predetermined conclusion — here, only pro-government data is cited while contradictory evidence is excluded. From Latin 'tendere' (to stretch or lean toward a goal), a tendentious argument always strains toward one side. Option C (logically inconsistent) is the key distractor: a tendentious report can be internally consistent — its flaw is bias in selection, not logical error. Option D (overly optimistic) mistakes tone for structural bias; TENDENTIOUS is about what evidence is chosen, not the emotional register. Grammar rule: TENDENTIOUS implies agenda-driven selectivity; it differs from 'inaccurate' (wrong facts) and 'opinionated' (merely expressing views). Another example: 'A TENDENTIOUS biography quotes only the subject's supporters and omits all critical voices.'

questions.stem: Constant political instability proved INIMICAL to the state's ambitions of becoming a leading destination for foreign investment. Choose the meaning of INIMICAL as used here.

options.option_text: irrelevant to and largely unnoticed by prospective investors
temporarily disruptive but ultimately not a serious deterrent
fundamentally hostile to and harmful for the stated ambition
unfairly blamed for problems caused entirely by other factors

questions.explanation: C is correct. INIMICAL means fundamentally opposed to and destructive of a goal — political instability does not merely slow investment attraction; it actively works against it as an enemy would. From Latin 'inimicus' (enemy, unfriendly; in- = not + amicus = friend). The causal sentence structure ('proved INIMICAL to ... ambitions') signals permanent, deep-seated harm, not incidental disruption. Option B (temporarily disruptive) is the most seductive distractor: 'disruptive' sounds severe, but INIMICAL implies systemic opposition by nature, not temporary inconvenience. Option A (irrelevant) is contradicted by the sentence's causal framing. Grammar rule: INIMICAL to X means X cannot coexist with it — they are constitutionally opposed, not just accidentally in conflict. Another example: 'Prolonged stress is INIMICAL to creative thinking, not merely a minor hindrance.'

questions.stem: What does VIVID mean as used in the sentence: 'The documentary offered a VIVID account of the 1947 partition, leaving viewers deeply shaken and emotional'?

options.option_text: producing a clear and powerfully striking impression
historically accurate but emotionally understated
slow-moving and heavily reliant on archive footage
factually detailed but purposely restrained in tone

questions.explanation: A is correct. The contextual clue is the emotional effect on viewers — the account is so sharp and lifelike that people feel shaken. VIVID here means 'producing a clear and powerfully striking impression', not merely accurate (B, D) or stylistically slow (C). Options B and D trap students who equate vivid with 'precise': accuracy is irrelevant; impact is the key. Etymology: Latin 'vividus' (lively), from 'vivere' (to live) — same root as 'vivacious'. Memory hook: a VIVID image is one that feels alive in the mind. Grammar rule: VIVID modifies the noun 'account' as an adjective and must be replaced by an adjective phrase, not a description of style or method.

questions.stem: Choose the phrase closest in meaning to CORDIAL as used in: 'Despite years of fierce competition, the two rival CEOs maintained a CORDIAL relationship at industry summits.'

options.option_text: outwardly polite but privately hostile in feeling
warm, sincere, and genuinely friendly in nature
strictly formal and carefully avoiding personal topics
superficially pleasant purely to serve business ends

questions.explanation: B is correct. CORDIAL signals genuine warmth; the phrase 'despite fierce competition' tells us the warmth endures beyond professional necessity, ruling out hidden hostility (A) or calculated pleasantness (D). Option C (strictly formal) is the most common distractor: students confuse professional politeness with cordiality, but cordial carries a warmth that mere formality lacks. Etymology: Latin 'cor/cordis' (heart) — same root as 'accord'. A cordial greeting comes from the heart, not from protocol. Grammar rule: CORDIAL is an attributive adjective; replacing it requires another adjective phrase that captures genuine warmth, not mere surface politeness.

questions.stem: The word PROLIFIC in the sentence below is best defined as: 'The PROLIFIC composer had written over two hundred symphonies, concertos, and chamber pieces before turning forty.'

options.option_text: widely acclaimed by critics and audiences equally
producing a remarkably large body of creative output
technically brilliant but increasingly repetitive over time
commercially successful across several distinct musical genres

questions.explanation: B is correct. The contextual anchor is 'over two hundred pieces' — sheer volume is the point, not quality, critical standing (A), style (C), or commercial reach (D). PROLIFIC means producing abundantly. Option A is the most seductive trap because excellence and prolific output often co-occur, but the sentence says nothing about acclaim. Etymology: Latin 'proles' (offspring) + 'facere' (to make) — literally 'producing offspring abundantly'. Memory hook: a PROLIFIC writer breeds books the way a prolific animal breeds young. Rule: always anchor your answer to the quantitative clue in the sentence, not to the positive connotations surrounding a word.

questions.stem: In the sentence below, TENUOUS can be replaced by which option without changing the contextual meaning: 'The entire campaign strategy rested on the TENUOUS assumption that voter turnout in rural districts would remain low.'?

options.option_text: fragile, poorly grounded, and easily undermined
controversial and actively disputed by political rivals
complex and dependent on multiple interconnected factors
bold, unconventional, and ultimately vindicated as correct

questions.explanation: A is correct. TENUOUS means thin and lacking substance; the strategy 'rests on' a fragile assumption — one crack and everything collapses. Option B (controversial) is the most common distractor: a tenuous claim is not necessarily disputed, it simply lacks solid grounding. The sentence shows no opposition — the flaw is internal weakness, not external challenge. Option C (complex) is the opposite of the 'thinness' implied by tenuous. Option D directly contradicts the word. Etymology: Latin 'tenuis' (thin) — same root as 'attenuate' (to make thin). Grammar rule: TENUOUS is an adjective meaning 'of little substance'; its substitute must also function as an adjective phrase conveying fragility, not controversy or complexity.

questions.stem: Which of the following best captures the meaning of AUSTERE as used: 'The mountain monastery followed an AUSTERE daily regimen — no meat, no music, no conversation after sundown.'?

options.option_text: spiritually demanding and deeply meditative in its aim
severely strict, allowing little comfort or indulgence
ancient, unchanged, and resistant to all outside influence
physically exhausting and unsuitable for elderly residents

questions.explanation: B is correct. The three examples — no meat, no music, no conversation — all denote deliberate removal of pleasures, which is precisely what AUSTERE means: severely plain and self-denying. Option A (spiritually demanding) is the most tempting trap: students associate monasteries with spirituality and choose A, but AUSTERE targets the regimen's severity, not its purpose. Option C conflates 'traditional' with 'austere'. Option D misreads the physical comfort angle. Etymology: Greek 'austeros' (harsh, bitter) — originally described rough, bitter-tasting wine. Rule: AUSTERE always implies deliberate removal of comfort or luxury; the context clues (the three negatives) are your guide, not the setting.

questions.stem: In which of the following sentences is GARRULOUS used in the same sense as in: 'The GARRULOUS vendor at the corner stall talked about unrelated matters for so long that customers silently slipped away'?

options.option_text: The garrulous professor's lectures were packed with carefully organised technical detail.
The garrulous guide rattled on about his own life, barely mentioning the monument.
The garrulous diplomat chose every word with deliberate and calculated precision.
The garrulous student asked sharp, incisive questions that impressed the interviewer.

questions.explanation: B is correct. In the source sentence GARRULOUS means excessively talkative about trivial or irrelevant matters — the vendor talks about unrelated things and drives customers away. Option B replicates both features: the guide talks about himself (irrelevant) and neglects the actual subject (excess irrelevance). Option A implies organised, detailed speech — the opposite of garrulous rambling. Option C implies precision and calculation, which contradict aimless chatter. Option D implies sharp insight, also opposite. The 'same sense' format demands matching both excess AND irrelevance, not just talkativeness. Etymology: Latin 'garrire' (to chatter) — same root as 'gargle', both involving repetitive, purposeless sound. Rule: identify the two contextual markers (EXCESS + IRRELEVANCE) and test each option against both before choosing.

questions.stem: The word INIMICAL is used in the passage to convey that: 'Years of rent-seeking behaviour and bureaucratic red tape proved INIMICAL to the region's startup ecosystem, driving talent abroad.'

options.option_text: the ecosystem was surprisingly resilient despite severe obstacles
the conditions were deeply harmful and actively opposed to growth
official policy was poorly designed but not deliberately damaging
external pressures mattered more than internal governance failures

questions.explanation: B is correct. INIMICAL means not merely harmful but actively hostile — it carries the sense of an opposing, enemy-like force. Rent-seeking and red tape are shown as forces working against growth and expelling talent, which matches 'deeply harmful and actively opposed to growth'. Option C is the most dangerous distractor: it concedes harm but removes the adversarial intensity of 'inimical', reducing it to mere negligence. Option A inverts the meaning entirely. Option D introduces a comparison absent from the passage. Etymology: Latin 'inimicus' (enemy) — same root as 'enemy' and 'enmity'. Memory hook: INIMICAL = 'enemy-like'; conditions that are inimical behave as enemies toward whatever they affect. Grammar rule: INIMICAL is typically followed by 'to' (inimical to growth), mirroring 'hostile to' and 'detrimental to' — all signal adversarial harm.

questions.stem: Choose the meaning of LUCID as used in the sentence: 'Her LUCID explanation of the tax reforms helped even the most confused voters understand the policy at once.'

options.option_text: expressed in a lively and highly entertaining way
expressed with complete clarity and ease of understanding
expressed with technical precision and mathematical accuracy
expressed in a forceful and emotionally persuasive manner

questions.explanation: B is correct. In context, LUCID describes the explanation as one that instantly cleared confusion — meaning clear and easy to understand. Etymology: Latin 'lucidus' (bright, shining with light). The word-formation principle: 'luc-' (light) → lucid, lucidity, elucidate all carry the sense of 'making bright/clear'. Option A (lively) is wrong — the context emphasises comprehension, not entertainment. Option C (technical precision) is the key distractor; but lucid is about simplicity of communication, not technical rigour. Another example: 'The judge gave a lucid summary of the verdict so that the layperson could follow it.' Memory hook: LUCID = like a torch in a dark room.

questions.stem: Choose the meaning of SCANT as used in: 'The investigating officer paid SCANT attention to the eyewitness account before closing the file prematurely.'

options.option_text: close and carefully recorded attention to all fine details
very little attention, barely sufficient or even inadequate
repeated and systematic attention spread over many sessions
formal and procedurally mandated attention required by law

questions.explanation: B is correct. 'Paid SCANT attention' is a fixed collocational phrase in English meaning gave very little or barely any attention. Etymology: Old Norse 'skamt' (short, brief). Word-formation rule: SCANT functions as an adjective meaning 'barely adequate in quantity'. Context clue: the file was closed 'prematurely', reinforcing the sense of insufficient attention. Option A (close attention) is the direct opposite. Option C (repeated attention) misreads 'scant' as a description of frequency rather than degree. Another example: 'The minister showed scant regard for the opposition's objections during the session.' Memory hook: SCANT = a SCANTY supply — barely enough.

questions.stem: Choose the meaning of FURTIVE as used in: 'She cast a FURTIVE glance at her colleague's answer sheet just before the invigilator turned around.'

options.option_text: a steady and openly confident look at something nearby
a quick, secretive look hinting at guilt or concealment
a long and admiringly curious look at another's work
a confused and uncertain look that lacked clear direction

questions.explanation: B is correct. FURTIVE implies stealth and secrecy, typically associated with doing something one should not. Etymology: Latin 'furtivus', from 'furtum' (theft) — one who acts like a thief sneaking about. Word-formation: the '-ive' suffix forms an adjective meaning 'characterised by'. Context clue: the action happens 'just before the invigilator turned around', confirming the concealment intent. Option A (openly confident) is the antonym. Option C (admiringly curious) removes the crucial element of guilt. Option D (confused) introduces an unrelated emotional state. Another example: 'The suspect made a furtive movement toward the exit when the detective mentioned the weapon.' Memory hook: FURTIVE rhymes with THEFT-ive — stealthy as a thief.

questions.stem: Choose the meaning of INVETERATE as used in: 'He was an INVETERATE gambler — no family crisis or financial ruin could keep him away from the card table for long.'

options.option_text: deeply habitual and long-established in behaviour, hard to reform
occasional and situational, only triggered by peer group pressure
professionally skilled and formally trained in the specific trade
emotionally driven and prone to sudden and reckless impulse acts

questions.explanation: A is correct. INVETERATE describes a habit so deeply rooted over time that it is resistant to change. Etymology: Latin 'inveteratus' — 'in-' (into) + 'vetus' (old) = 'made old within', i.e., long-ingrained. Word-formation: the '-ate' past-participial suffix signals a completed, settled condition. Context clue: 'no family crisis or financial ruin could keep him away' confirms the habit is entrenched and long-standing. Option B (occasional) directly contradicts the deep-rootedness. Option C (professionally trained) confuses habitual practice with formal skill. Option D (emotional impulsiveness) misses the time-depth element that INVETERATE carries. Another example: 'She was an inveterate reader — even power cuts could not stop her from reaching for a book.' Memory hook: INVETERATE = IN-VETERAN = old veteran of a habit.

questions.stem: Choose the meaning of EPHEMERAL as used in: 'Social media fame proved EPHEMERAL — the viral video had millions of views one week and was completely forgotten the next.'

options.option_text: intensely powerful yet concentrated within a very narrow audience
lasting for only a brief period before vanishing quickly away
broadly popular across many different age groups and income levels
difficult to measure or quantify through any reliable standard method

questions.explanation: B is correct. EPHEMERAL means short-lived or transitory. Etymology: Greek 'ephemeros' — 'epi' (upon/for) + 'hemera' (day) = lasting only a day. Word-formation: many scientific terms use 'hemera-' (day-related). Context clue: 'millions of views one week… completely forgotten the next' precisely illustrates something that vanishes quickly. Option A (narrow audience) misreads the context and ignores the temporal element. Option C (broadly popular) contradicts the rapid disappearance. Option D (difficult to measure) introduces an irrelevant idea of quantification. Another example: 'The ephemeral beauty of cherry blossoms draws millions of visitors every spring in Japan.' Memory hook: EPHEMERAL — think 'a day's duration' (hemera = day, as in ephemeris).

questions.stem: Choose the meaning of EQUIVOCATE as used in: 'When directly asked about the missing procurement funds, the treasurer began to EQUIVOCATE, offering vague half-answers that satisfied nobody in the room.'

options.option_text: to speak with deliberate ambiguity in order to avoid full commitment
to restate the same denial repeatedly in slightly reworded language
to raise procedural or technical objections that deflect the main issue
to concede partial wrongdoing while firmly denying the core accusation

questions.explanation: A is correct. EQUIVOCATE means to use ambiguous language deliberately in order to mislead or to avoid committing to a clear position. Etymology: Latin 'aequi' (equal) + 'vox/vocare' (voice/to call) — literally 'to call in two equal directions simultaneously', i.e., to say something that could be taken either way. Word-formation: '-ate' is the verbal suffix; 'equi-' appears in equidistant, equilateral (equal on all sides). Context clue: 'vague half-answers that satisfied nobody' directly captures ambiguity-without-commitment. Option B (restate the same denial) is prevarication, a related but distinct act — repetition, not ambiguity. Option C (procedural objections) describes a different evasion strategy altogether. Option D (partial concession) is a specific admission strategy, the opposite of equivocation's deliberate vagueness. Another example: 'The politician equivocated on the tax hike, refusing to say yes or no when pressed by the journalist.' Memory hook: EQUIVOCATE = EQUAL + VOICE = speaking in two equal directions at once — saying nothing clearly.

questions.stem: Choose the meaning of TENDENTIOUS as used in: 'The opposition leaders labelled the government-funded documentary TENDENTIOUS, arguing that it had cherry-picked data to advance a predetermined political narrative.'

options.option_text: promoting a particular agenda in a biased and one-sided fashion
relying heavily on unverified rumours and anonymous secondhand claims
deploying emotionally manipulative imagery designed to exploit public grief
presenting accurate facts in a dull and unnecessarily complicated format

questions.explanation: A is correct. TENDENTIOUS describes writing or speech that promotes a particular cause or point of view in a biased, partial way — it appears balanced but is not. Etymology: from Latin 'tendere' (to stretch, to aim at) + '-ious' (adjectival suffix) — something that stretches toward a fixed end. Word-formation rule: 'tend-' root appears in tendency, tendentious, contend, intend — all carry the sense of aiming or leaning toward something. Context clue: 'cherry-picked data to advance a predetermined political narrative' exactly describes tendentious presentation. Option B (unverified rumours) is closer to fabrication or gossip — TENDENTIOUS does not imply falsity, only selective bias. Option C (emotional manipulation) describes pathos-heavy rhetoric, not the selective-evidence bias of tendentious argument. Option D (accurate but dull) is the opposite — TENDENTIOUS is deliberately skewed, not merely dry. Another example: 'The historian's tendentious account of the Partition portrayed one community as entirely responsible for the violence.' Memory hook: TENDENTIOUS = has a strong TENDENCY — it always leans the same way, by design.

questions.stem: Choose the meaning of LUCID as used in the sentence: 'Despite the complexity of quantum mechanics, the teacher offered a LUCID account that even beginners could follow.'

options.option_text: filled with vivid imagery and memorable metaphors
expressed with striking clarity and easy to follow
lengthy and packed with specialised technical terms
abstract and deliberately challenging to interpret

questions.explanation: B is correct. 'Lucid' derives from Latin 'lucidus' (bright, lit up) and in context means clear and intelligible — the account is easy to follow, not ornate or complex. Option A ('vivid imagery') confuses lucid with 'evocative'; a lucid text may be plain, not picturesque. Option C is the opposite: a lucid account is concise, not jargon-heavy. Option D is the antonym. Grammar rule: when a modifier like 'even beginners could follow' follows the noun, it defines the quality in context — here, accessibility, not depth or imagery. Another example: 'She gave a lucid summary of the 300-page bill in just five minutes.'

questions.stem: Choose the meaning of FRUGAL as used in the sentence: 'The retired schoolmaster led a FRUGAL life, buying only what was essential and saving every spare rupee.'

options.option_text: extremely poor and unable to meet basic daily needs
careful with money and avoiding all needless expense
generous in sharing earnings with those less fortunate
strict and rigidly self-disciplined in all habits

questions.explanation: B is correct. 'Frugal' comes from Latin 'frugalis' (virtuous, economical) and here signals a deliberate, voluntary economy — not poverty. Option A (unable to afford basics) confuses frugal with 'destitute'; the key difference is choice vs compulsion. The phrase 'buying only what was essential' confirms intentional restraint, not inability. Option C is the near-antonym; a frugal person saves, not gives away. Option D (self-disciplined) is tempting because frugal people appear disciplined, but 'frugal' is specifically about money management, not general lifestyle strictness. Rule: Context clues like 'saving every spare rupee' anchor the word to its financial-economy sense, overriding any broader meaning. Another example: 'Lata Mangeshkar was famously frugal despite her enormous wealth.'

questions.stem: Choose the meaning of TENACIOUS as used in the sentence: 'The lawyer's TENACIOUS pursuit of justice kept the appeal alive for three gruelling years in court.'

options.option_text: aggressively combative and inclined toward verbal conflict
holding firm with persistent and unwavering determination
legally brilliant and technically unmatched in courtroom
driven purely by financial reward and personal ambition

questions.explanation: B is correct. 'Tenacious' derives from Latin 'tenax' (holding fast, gripping) and in context describes the quality of not letting go — the appeal survived three years because the lawyer refused to quit. Option C is the most seductive distractor: brilliant lawyers are often tenacious, but the sentence stresses the duration of effort ('three gruelling years'), not skill level. Option A ('combative') is wrong; tenacious is about persistence, not aggression. Option D misreads motive — the sentence focuses on the outcome (justice), not reward. Grammar rule: the noun phrase 'pursuit of justice' reveals the direction of the tenacity; the word modifies effort sustained over time, not manner of argument. Another example: 'A tenacious vine will crack through concrete to reach sunlight.'

questions.stem: Choose the meaning of NEFARIOUS as used in the sentence: 'The inquiry exposed a NEFARIOUS scheme through which officials had siphoned public funds into private accounts.'

options.option_text: hidden and deliberately concealed from watchdog bodies
wicked, criminal, and morally indefensible in character
highly organised with clearly distributed corrupt roles
financially fraudulent but not involving physical harm

questions.explanation: B is correct. 'Nefarious' comes from Latin 'nefas' (sin, crime against divine law) and carries a strong moral condemnation — it is not merely secretive or organised, but fundamentally wicked. Option A ('hidden') is the top distractor because corrupt schemes are indeed concealed, but 'nefarious' targets the moral quality, not the method of concealment; 'clandestine' would fit A. Option C describes structure, not ethics. Option D is too narrow — nefarious encompasses all serious moral crimes, not just nonviolent fraud. Rule: When 'nefarious' modifies 'scheme', the sentence frames wrongdoing as both criminal and morally reprehensible, not merely procedurally irregular. Another example: 'The villain hatched a nefarious plot to poison the city's water supply.'

questions.stem: Choose the meaning of DISPARATE as used in the sentence: 'The reform committee drew members from DISPARATE fields — medicine, law, farming, and finance — making consensus elusive.'

options.option_text: hostile to one another because of competing interests
fundamentally different in kind with almost nothing in common
spread unevenly across many different geographic regions
unequal in political power and institutional influence

questions.explanation: B is correct. 'Disparate' derives from Latin 'disparatus' (set apart, separated) and means essentially different in nature — medicine and farming share no common professional vocabulary or methodology. Option A ('hostile') is wrong; disparate groups may coexist amicably but think differently — 'making consensus elusive' refers to intellectual divergence, not animosity. Option C confuses disparate with 'dispersed' (geographically scattered). Option D confuses it with 'unequal' (hierarchical difference); disparate groups can be equal in status but differ in kind. Grammar rule: the enumeration 'medicine, law, farming, and finance' illustrates the word by contrast — each item belongs to a completely different domain. Another example: 'The report tried to reconcile disparate findings from ten independent surveys.'

questions.stem: Choose the meaning of INSOUCIANT as used in the sentence: 'While the rest of the cabinet appeared shaken by the censure motion, the minister remained INSOUCIANT, joking casually with reporters outside.'

options.option_text: deliberately hiding anxiety so as to project inner confidence
displaying a breezy, carefree unconcern for trouble ahead
fully aware of the threat but calmly resigned to the outcome
emboldened by political allies and a secure electoral base

questions.explanation: B is correct. 'Insouciant' is borrowed from French (in- 'not' + soucier 'to care') and means a genuine, light-hearted lack of worry — the minister is not suppressing alarm but truly unbothered. Option A ('hiding anxiety') is the sharpest distractor; it imagines a performance of calm, whereas insouciant implies the absence of worry itself. Option C ('resigned') suggests stoic acceptance of inevitable bad news; insouciant carries no such heaviness. Option D ('emboldened by allies') gives a strategic reason for confidence, whereas insouciant implies emotional detachment regardless of circumstances. Etymology mnemonic: think 'in-sou-ciant' → 'no care in the soul.' Another example: 'She gave an insouciant shrug when the critics panned her debut novel.'

questions.stem: Choose the meaning of ABSTRUSE as used in the sentence: 'The philosopher's later monographs grew increasingly ABSTRUSE, and even her doctoral students confessed they could not follow every argument.'

options.option_text: written in a style heavy with specialised technical vocabulary
obscure and difficult to grasp owing to profound complexity
deliberately provocative and designed to invite controversy
employing an outdated idiom no longer current in scholarship

questions.explanation: B is correct. 'Abstruse' derives from Latin 'abstrusus' (pushed away, concealed) and describes ideas so deeply complex that they become inaccessible — the difficulty lies in the reasoning, not the vocabulary. Option A is the trickiest distractor: dense jargon does make texts hard, but 'abstruse' points to the depth of the ideas themselves, not to word choice; a text can be abstruse in plain English. Option D describes 'archaic' writing — old-fashioned diction, not intellectual opacity. Option C describes 'contentious' or 'polemic' work; abstruse carries no deliberate intent to provoke. The contextual clue 'doctoral students could not follow every argument' confirms the difficulty is conceptual, not linguistic. Etymology hook: abstract + recuse → 'pulled away from easy reach.' Another example: 'Einstein's field equations were abstruse even to most physicists in 1915.'
